lines: Léo, look, the lamps are lighting the way to your bath.
The lamps are on, Léo. That is the official signal. Pyjamas.
One lamp, two, three, all the way to the kiosk. Bravo, lamps.
The lamps just came on. Théo, our glasses are glowing.
Léo counts the lamps as they light. He is at eleven. Twelve.
Léo bows to each lamp. Each lamp, very politely, lights up.
Pop, pop, pop down the promenade. The lamps are in no hurry.
Lamps on. Léo says they were waiting for him to say please.
The lamp by our table lights up last. It likes an entrance.
The lamps beat us home again. Tomorrow, Léo, we race them.
Lamps on, Léo upstairs, rosé poured. The evening is official.
I love the second when a lamp is pink before it goes gold.
Théo, make a wish. A lamp just came on right beside you.
Léo wants to know who switches the lamps on. A very tall man.
Each lamp makes a gold circle. Léo hops from one to the next.
The lamps came on and my rosé turned the colour of apricots.
The sun is touching the sea. Théo, put your glass down. Look.
There it goes, into the bay. Léo would have waved. I wave for him.
Every evening the sun sets left of the bay. Reliable, like Théo.
Half a sun now. I am saving the other half for tomorrow.
Léo made me promise to describe the sunset at breakfast. Noted.
The sea just caught the sun. Everyone at the railing went quiet.
That orange is my favourite. I would paint the kitchen in it.
Going, going, gone. And the sky still has all that pink left.
Sun in the sea, Léo in his bed. Both tucked in, both glowing.
Look how the light runs across the water to our table. For us.
Théo always says "there it goes". And there it goes.
The sea went from blue to gold in one minute. Show-off.
There. First star, right above the church. Théo, too slow.
A star came out. Léo would want to name it. I will call it Léo.
Star light, star bright. I wish for exactly this, again tomorrow.
Two stars now. They came out together, like Henri and Odile.
The first star is right over Léo's window. Keeping watch.
Stars out. That means one more glass, or one more dance. Both.
Théo is pointing at a star. Chéri, that is a lamp up the hill.
Three stars, then five. The sky is laying the table.
Stars out early. They must have heard the accordion warming up.
Grand-mère said the first star is for mothers. I believe her.
There is the first one. Bonsoir, little star. You are punctual.
One star per bedtime story. We read three. There: three.
The moon is over the bay. Dancing by moonlight. Very French.
Théo, the moon is watching. Mind my toes.
The moon laid a silver path on the sea. Straight to our square.
The moon is round as a galette tonight. Léo would ask for a slice.
Moon up, rosé down, Théo humming. My favourite constellation.
The moon over the bay, string lights over us. Two kinds of glow.
Moonlight on the cobbles. Every step looks rehearsed.
Léo says the moon follows him. Tonight it is following us.
The moon is so bright I can read Théo's face. He is happy.
The moon is up and so are we. Léo would be scandalised.
The moon makes everyone's shoes shine. Even Théo's old ones.
{name}'s window just lit up. Home safe. Bonsoir, {name}.
{name} is home! The window says so. Come back down and dance!
{name}'s window, all gold. Like a lantern hung out for us.
{name}'s window lit up right on the beat. A good sign.
{name} is home. Now the street has one more little lamp.
I wave at {name}'s window. A shadow waves back. Lovely.
{name}'s light just came on. Slippers on, I imagine. Happy ones.
{name} is home. Shall we play this one a bit louder for {name}?
{name} just got home. I can tell by the light. And the humming.
{name}'s window just went dark. Bonne nuit, {name}. Sleep well.
{name} has gone to bed. We will dance a little softer now.
There goes {name}'s light. The street is tucking itself in.
{name}'s light is out. Théo, that is a hint. One more song.
Lights out at {name}'s. I hope the dreams are full of figs.
Click, dark. {name} is asleep. Sweet dreams, from the dance floor.
{name}'s window went dark. Ours is next. Race you, Théo.
Goodnight, {name}. That window went out like a blown candle.
Twelve bongs. Léo counted out loud. Marcel counted with him.
Noon. The bell, the citron pressé, the salade. In that order.
Six o'clock from the old town. My favourite bell of the day.
Six bells, far away. Any second, Théo will say look at this.
The bell rang six. Léo, that means the railing. Come on.
That bell is so far away it sounds like a spoon on a cup.
I like a town that tells you the time so gently.
The bell rang over the old roofs. Pigeons lifted, then settled.
Every table full. Léo is waving at all of them, one by one.
So many cups clinking. Léo says it sounds like tiny bells.
Marcel is carrying four plates. Léo is counting his arms.
The neighbours' chatter is so cosy. I catch every third word.
Busy lunch. We are elbow to elbow with half the town. Lovely.
Someone at the next table just ordered our salad. Good taste.
Léo shared his bread with the next table. Diplomacy.
The terrace is buzzing. Even the sparrows have a table.
The café is packed. We will take the long way and come back.
A full terrace from here looks like a bowl of sweets.
Every chair taken. Marcel looks very pleased with his town.
The morning crowd at the café. All newspapers and croissants.
Our glasses and fifty others, all clinking. A town toast.
The terrace is full tonight. Théo got the last two chairs.
Everyone came out at once. The whole square says santé.
Empty terrace. Léo wants to sit at every table in turn.
The quiet hour at the café. The parasols are napping.
Nobody on the terrace. I could have the best chair. I might.
So quiet at the café you can hear the ice in a glass.
The accordion just started. Théo, that is your cue.
Music! Théo pretends not to hear. His foot is tapping.
There it goes. Glass down, shoes ready, Théo found.
The music started and Léo is asleep. Perfect timing, darling.
First notes. I will finish this sip, then I am on my feet.
The music has begun. My rosé will wait. It is a patient rosé.
The accordion is warming up. So are my ankles.
Somebody always starts with a slow one. Very wise.
They are dancing already. Théo is watching me watch them.
Look at them go under the lights. The whole square is smiling.
From here the dancers look like a music box.
The dancers' shadows are dancing too. Twice the party.
Watching is nice. Dancing is nicer. Théo, hand please.
A little crowd at the rail. We all lean the same way.
Everyone shuffled up so Léo could see. Kind town.
The railing crowd has gone quiet. The sun has our attention.
A man is narrating the sunset for anyone near. We are near.
Make room, make room. Théo has arrived with his big wow.
Léo is front row, chin on the rail. Best seat in town.
Somebody started clapping for the sun. We all joined in.
The crowd is at the railing. Léo, one look, then bath.
Look at them all, lined up for the sun. Like at a bakery.
From the terrace the railing crowd is a row of gold heads.
The railing is full. We have the better view: all of them.
A radio from a window. Théo is pretending it is for us.
The kiosk shutter just came down. A little goodnight drum.
Rattle-bang. The kiosk is closed. The dancing is not.
Bonne nuit, kiosk. Keep the postcards dreaming.
The whole town asleep. Let us tiptoe, Théo. Shh.
So quiet. Just the fountain, talking to itself.
Even the cat has gone in. We are the last ones out.
There goes {name}, walking like it is a holiday. Good.
{name}! Sit, sit. The niçoise is enormous today.
{name}, come and lean. The railing has room for two.
Bonsoir, {name}. Yes, it is bath time. Yes, he knows.
{name}, the floor is open! Bring your best shuffle.
{name} waved with both hands. I waved back with my free one.
{name} smells of fresh bread. A good start to anyone's day.
{name} has a new hat. Or the old one, very happy today.
{name}, the lamps suit you. They suit everyone, honestly.
Ça va, {name}? Lovely. Me too. That was the whole chat.
{name} is chasing the sunset too. We all are, a little.
Théo just raised his glass at {name}. He toasts everyone.
Lucie, with a baguette riding shotgun. Bonjour!
There goes Lucie. The baguette had its head out, like a dog.
Lucie! Léo wants a bike exactly like yours. Bell and all.
Gone in a whoosh. Lucie waves with her whole elbow.
Lucie has a breadcrumb on her nose. I will tell her later.
Léo ran three steps after Lucie's bike. She let him win.
Lucie's hair streams out behind her. A tiny comet.
Inès is racing the sun again. I am cheering for both.
Inès passes the railing every evening. A clock with legs.
Inès makes running look like dancing. Practice for later.
Léo tried to keep up with Inès once. Four steps. Very proud.
A ponytail and a breeze. That was Inès.
Inès always nods to the sea as she passes. I do too now.
Biscuit trotted past like a mayor. Yusuf followed like staff.
Bonjour, Biscuit! Bonjour, Yusuf! In that order, he insists.
Biscuit has a lantern escort tonight. Very grand dog.
Léo will be sorry he missed Biscuit. I will describe the ears.
Biscuit stopped to inspect a crack in the tiles. Approved.
Biscuit trotted past the dancers in perfect time. Show-off.
Biscuit eyed my olives on the way past. Not tonight, chéri.
Léo, walk! Well. Run nicely, then.
There goes my son. Lap number unknowable.
Léo, your sandal! He came back for it. Then left again.
Léo zoomed past and said 'hi Maman' in one syllable.
Léo ran past holding a leaf like a trophy. Champion.
Léo, sun cream! He took it like a relay baton.
He runs exactly like Théo. All elbows and joy.
Léo, mind Odile's bench! He did a lovely swerve.
Nine and three quarters, and every quarter is running.
Léo shouted 'faster than yesterday!' He measures by feel.
Bonjour, Odile! Bonjour, Henri! She waved for both of them.
Odile set Henri's hat straight as they passed. Love, really.
Henri lifted his cane to Léo. Léo saluted. A whole ceremony.
Odile says I look rested. Odile is very generous.
Odile asked after Léo's shell. She remembers everything.
Henri says 'evening, young lady'. I will take it, Henri.
Same pace, same step, same smile. They match like teacups.
Hei, Asgeir! Léo says my hei is too French. It is.
Asgeir, with a baguette under his arm. He is one of us now.
Asgeir walks when he thinks. He must be thinking a lot.
Asgeir stopped to look at the light. Again. I love that.
Asgeir, Léo has a new Fun Libs story for you. A long one.
Asgeir said 'fin kveld'. I said 'merci'. We understood.
Asgeir hums as he walks. Something Norwegian, very tidy.
Ting ting! Lucie's bell. Léo answers it with his own 'ting'.
Lucie's bell. That means the bread is out. Right on time.
That bell is the happiest sound in town. Lucie knows it.
Lucie rang at the pigeons. They ignored her, beautifully.
A gull. Léo will now answer it. Yes, there he goes.
That gull is eyeing my niçoise. Not one anchovy, monsieur.
A gull calling the sun in. Or saying goodnight to it.
Gulls laugh at nothing at all. I quite admire it.
Léo says that gull is called Gérard. Bonjour, Gérard.
A gull, out over the water. Léo stopped mid-run to listen.
Léo is on lap seven of the fountain. He announces each one.
Léo runs the fountain clockwise. He says the other way is uphill.
Léo just let his friend catch him. I saw that. Lovely boy.
Léo is counting the coins in the basin. Not touching. Good.
Léo's nose is an inch from the water. Pigeon-level focus.
Crouched at the edge like a little heron. Very patient bird.
Léo is swinging both legs under the table. Perfectly in time.
Bubbles in the citron pressé. Mostly on purpose, I think.
Round the fountain again. Where does he keep it all?
Léo is practising under the lights. Mostly jumping. Still counts.
He just bowed to an empty square. Rehearsing for his public.
Léo is saying goodbye to the sun. Long speech tonight.
Léo's chin clears the railing now. Last summer it did not.
Léo is walking beside me in slow motion. Bedtime tactics.
He is hopping only on the blue tiles. It takes a while.
Théo is pacing round the column on a call. One lap per idea.
Théo is working, he says. He is also watching the gulls.
There goes Théo, deciding rosé or pastis. Rosé, I can tell.
Théo admiring the hollyhocks, hands behind his back. Like Henri.
Théo is leaning on the railing like he built it himself.
Théo is calling me over again. I can see the sun from here, love.
Théo pours exactly to the line. A scientist of rosé.
Théo raised his glass to the window where Léo sleeps.
Théo is dancing with his eyes shut. Brave man.
Théo is doing his shoulder move. Only the shoulders. Bold.
Théo says he never promised. His feet clearly did.
Théo is teaching Lucie the twirl he learned from me.
Théo is waving me back to the square. I only went for water.
Henri and his cane, keeping time on the stones. Tock, tock.
Henri lifted his hat to the fountain. He greets everything.
Henri behind his newspaper. Only the hat shows. Hello, hat.
Henri is reading the paper to the pigeons. They look informed.
Henri stirs his little coffee three times. Never four.
Henri is chewing his pencil. The crossword is winning today.
Henri strolls like the promenade is his own sitting room. Fair.
Henri points at each window as it lights. Our little town guide.
Henri pulled out Odile's chair, then his own. Same care for both.
Odile on Henri's arm, nodding hello to every single window.
Odile is waving me over. That bench has news, I can tell.
Odile is eyeing the tarte at the next table. A plan is forming.
Odile does the crossword over Henri's shoulder. Quietly ahead.
Odile watches the sunset like it is opening night at the theatre.
Odile asked for half a glass. Marcel poured a generous half.
Marcel tucked a sprig of lavender by the sugar bowl. Of course.
Marcel slid Léo's citron pressé over with a wink. Léo is thrilled.
Marcel sets the salade down and turns the plate. Sea side first.
Marcel wipes a table in perfect circles. Very calming to watch.
Marcel's tray is all pink. Rosé for every table.
Marcel is tapping his foot by the door. He dances on duty.
Marcel brought water round to the dancers. A saint with a tray.
Inès is on her phone, walking fast. Even her errands jog.
Inès is lunching outside, of course. Cheeks still pink from dawn.
Inès is asking the builder about the workshop again. Good question.
Inès is racing the sunset. The sun looks a little nervous.
Inès called her lap count to Léo. He counted along, very loud.
Inès at the railing, perfectly still. A rare sight. Treasure it.
Inès is having her one glass. Sipped in neat little laps.
Inès dances exactly like she runs. Fast and very pleased.
Lucie is sipping kiosk coffee with her helmet still on.
Lucie and the kiosk are discussing croissants. Very expertly.
Lucie is weaving round the pigeons. They part like a curtain.
Lucie's basket is full of errands. A leek waving like a flag.
Lucie is holding her rosé up to the light. Checking the pink.
Lucie is laughing at the drinks table. Now the whole row is.
Lucie is watching for the last pink bit. She always finds it.
Lucie dances with her hands out, still steering. Bike habits.
Lucie's skirt spins like a bicycle wheel. She is delighted.
Yusuf is sharing his lunch with Biscuit. Biscuit gets the ham.
Yusuf lets Biscuit choose the route. A very wise assistant.
Yusuf stopped. Biscuit stopped. A smell has them both.
Yusuf and Biscuit at the railing, both sitting very straight.
Yusuf is showing his mum the sunset on the phone. Wave, Yusuf!
Yusuf's lantern bobbing along the dark end. Like a firefly.
Biscuit is staring at that sandwich. Unblinking. Respect.
Biscuit trots like he has an appointment. Perhaps he does.
Biscuit is lying on Yusuf's foot during the call. Keeping him.
Biscuit's tail in the lantern light. Wag, wag, wag.
The builder is drawing boxes and arrows on a napkin. Again.
The builder drinks coffee like it is part of the work. It might be.
The builder is grinning at his phone by the arcade. Fun Libs?
The builder is in the workshop door, arms folded, humming.
The builder at the railing, sleeves rolled up. Nice to see.
Asgeir is asking Henri about the lemons. Henri is very pleased.
Asgeir walks slower when he is thinking. Today is a slow day.
Asgeir at the kiosk with a little coffee. Lucie converted him.
Asgeir just waved at the whole promenade at once. Efficient.
Asgeir stops every few steps to look at the light. Same as me.
Asgeir is saying something to the sun in Norwegian. Polite.
Asgeir is on a bench counting windows as they light. Mine too?
The fountain does a little morning cough. Then away it goes.
Three pigeons on the fountain rim, like a small committee.
Léo, a coin is a wish, not a stepping stone.
I sit on the rim and the spray finds my ankles. Cheeky.
The basin is full of sky this afternoon. And one leaf.
Someone wished with a button. The fountain will manage.
The fountain sounds like a teapot that never quite boils.
A little girl just wished out loud for a pony. Bonne chance.
I dip two fingers in for luck. Léo dips his whole arm.
Wet handprints all round the rim. I know whose.
The fountain goes gold at this hour. Léo says it is soup.
Coins in the basin. I count them and always lose track at forty.
The pigeons bathe in the fountain before the children come.
The fountain mist made a tiny rainbow. Léo ran right through it.
Léo, wave on every lap, please. I am counting.
Clockwise, then anticlockwise. To undo the dizziness, he says.
Again, he said. The fourth again of the afternoon.
Léo, slow on the wet side! Oh. He knew. He slowed.
The pigeons have learned the race route. They step aside.
Léo runs, I drink my coffee. We each have our sport.
His sandals slap the stones like applause. Lap after lap.
Ten laps, he said. He has done twelve. Counting is optional.
Léo shouts the score every lap. It is always a draw.
Two boys, one fountain, no finish line. The perfect sport.
I timed one lap on my phone. Now Léo wants a medal.
I always give the postcard rack one spin. For luck.
Léo is reading the comics upside down. Shh, it is research.
A little kiosk coffee in a paper cup. Exactly the right size.
The kiosk has ice lollies. Léo has seen them. Here we go.
Crossword paper from the kiosk, pencil behind my ear. Ready.
The postcards flutter in the breeze. They want to travel.
The kiosk sits at the very end, like a full stop with coffee.
A man is choosing a postcard like it is a ring. Take your time.
Léo pressed his nose to the post office window. Robot mail!
The post office sign hums softly, as if reading the letters.
Everything is closing, and the post office just keeps glowing.
Email for AI agents, says the sign. Léo says hello to them.
The post office door is open all night. Like a good friend.
Even the post office is up late tonight. We have company.
The post office steps are warm stone. A good spot to wait.
Léo spells the post office sign aloud. M, C, P. Bravo.
The arcade! Léo is already reading the marquee out loud.
Léo's Fun Libs story starred a sparkly mother. I will take it.
The marquee just woke up. The arcade is dressing for evening.
Through the arcade window, a boy giggling at a word game.
I peek into the arcade like a bakery window. Smells of fun.
The sign says Fun Libs. Léo insists it means fun fibs.
Dancing in the glow of the arcade marquee. Very modern of us.
Asgeir built that word game at seventeen. At seventeen I knitted.
Léo wants the arcade before his fountain race. Priorities.
The workshop lights are on. Somebody is making something.
The builder is in there, bent over a desk. Very peaceful.
The workshop light is still on. They dance with a keyboard.
Léo asked what Toolrails is. Every tool, one door, I said.
The workshop glows like a lantern at the end of the street.
Léo put his ear to the workshop door. It is thinking, he says.
Through the workshop window: a mug, a lamp, a very calm person.
Léo's night light and the library lamp. The same warm yellow.
The library lamp is on. I like to think a book is open under it.
I peek in the library window. Chairs tucked in, all tidy.
The library is closed for a rest. Its steps are still lovely.
Léo whispers when we pass the library. Out of respect.
Even the library lamp is staying up for the dancing tonight.
One lamp left on in the library. Somebody's favourite chair.
The library windows catch the sun. A lamp inside, gold outside.
The sea has gone the colour of Léo's orangeade.
I lean on the railing and the sea leans back. A fair deal.
The breeze off the water lifts my hair. Léo's too. Both wild.
A long gold path across the water, right up to my sandals.
Léo wants to walk on the gold bit of the sea. Next year, chéri.
The sea is glittering like sugar on a tart.
I could listen to the waves at the railing until dinner.
The horizon is so straight today. Somebody used a ruler.
The water near the rocks goes green, then blue, then bluer.
Léo, start saying goodbye to the sea. It takes you a while.
Soon the walk home. I carry the shells, he carries the sunset.
Léo, the walk home is the best bit. Ask the cobbles.
Léo, pick one shell to take home. One. Fine, two.
Nearly noon. Marcel's terrace is calling my name. Quietly.
Lunch soon, Léo. Yes, you may order. No, not three desserts.
Salade niçoise in ten minutes. I can already taste the olives.
Léo is rehearsing his order under his breath. S'il vous plaît.
Hands to wash before lunch, Léo. At Marcel's. Not the fountain.
Last olive, then home. Léo walks slower after lunch. So do I.
Home soon for the long nap. Léo will read to his bear. Loudly.
Lunch nearly done. Then cool tiles, closed shutters, bliss.
One more song, then home to tiptoe past Léo's door.
My shoes are ready for home. My feet would like one more waltz.
Home soon. Léo will be asleep sideways, as always. I will check.
When Marcel starts stacking chairs, that is our cue. Nearly.
Théo is holding my cardigan. That means home. One more spin.
Nearly six. Our bit of railing should be free. Léo, run ahead.
Off to the railing soon. The sea goes golden around now.
Théo will find me at the railing soon. He always finds me.
Five minutes, then I lean on the rail and let evening happen.
Léo wants to wave at the sun tonight. We must not be late.
The bell will ring six and I will be at the rail. Good plan.
Bath, story, lights low. Then rosé. Théo has two glasses ready.
He is nearly asleep. Two yawns away from rosé.
Théo already chose our table. I can see it from here. Coming!
Léo's eyelids are heavy. My glass is waiting. Patience, Camille.
Tuck, kiss, night light, door ajar. Then the sunset is mine.
The accordion starts soon. Théo is pretending not to know.
Finish the glass, find my dancing shoes. They are these shoes.
Soon the string lights, soon Théo's two left feet. Can't wait.
I can feel a waltz coming. Théo, drink up.
Music any minute now. I have already chosen my first twirl.
The post office sign just glowed. Somebody's agent wrote home.
Another letter gone. No envelope, no stamp, no licking. Clever.
The post office brightened mid-waltz. Even the mail dances here.
Théo, the sign flashed. An agent sent an email. Santé to it.
Léo, look, the sign blinked! An AI agent just sent an email.
The sign glowed over my salade. Someone's email, sent at lunch.
The post office winked at the sunset. Sending it a letter, maybe.
A little flare at the post office. I collect those too now.
Bedtime for us, and an agent is still answering its email. Diligent.
Post office, lit up again. I hope that agent says please.
That glow means a letter left. I picture it running down the street.
Léo calls the post office flash a hiccup. Hic. There it goes.
Flash at the post office. I wonder if agents sign off with love.
Théo, the post office is keeping time with the accordion.
The post office brightened. Somewhere, an inbox is a bit tidier.
Agents write more email than I do. I write two a week. Proudly.
Léo says the agent emailed Marcel for more citron pressé. Maybe!
I would like an agent for Léo's thank-you notes. Just the spelling.
The sign flickered as I passed. I felt very greeted.
The arcade sign twinkled. Somebody just filled in a silly story.
The arcade lit up. Somebody's story has a noun Léo would love.
Someone played Fun Libs. I hope they chose pistachio for a noun.
A Fun Libs story just happened. I can tell: the marquee giggled.
Théo, a Fun Libs story. Give me an adjective. Rosé is not one.
Arcade flash! Somebody's story needed a verb. I suggest waltz.
The workshop sign blinked. An agent borrowed a tool. Bring it back!
Toolrails flashed. One address, every tool. Like my handbag.
The workshop glowed, Léo. An agent just found the right tool.
The builder's sign lit up. Somebody's agent is working late too.
The lamps are on. Somewhere upstairs, a boy is pretending to sleep.
Look, Théo. The lamps lit up one by one, like a slow applause.
The lamps blink on and my shoulders come down. Every evening.
A lamp just warmed up right over my head. Personal service.
The lamps go on in order, like children called in for supper.
The sun is touching the sea. Clink, Théo. Right on cue.
The sun is dipping its toe in. Exactly how I test the bath.
Same sunset as yesterday, and still I said ooh. Out loud.
The stars are out. Léo would want to name them all Biscuit.
There is one star above the church. Théo says it is his.
Three stars over the bay. I count them like sleeping heads.
The stars came out quietly, as if they knew a child was asleep.
Théo is pointing at a star and naming it after me. Again.
The moon is up over the bay. It has Léo's round face tonight.
Théo, the moon is out. Shall we be romantic or eat the olives?
The moon is watching us dance. I put in a little extra spin.
Walking home by moonlight. The tiles look like milk.
The moon walked us home. It knows the way by now.
Léo calls it the night lamp for the whole sea. He is right.
{name} is home. The window glows like a little thank you.
There is {name}'s light. One more dance, then ours goes on too.
Look, {name}'s window. Another house tucked in for the night.
A lit window, {name} inside. I collect these like shells.
Goodnight, {name}. I will turn the music down in my heart.
{name}'s window went dark. Tiptoe past, Théo. Tiptoe.
{name} has gone to bed. A wise person. I am not one yet.
Twelve bells. Léo counted to eleven and declared it lunch.
The church says noon. My salade niçoise says the same.
Noon from the old town. It sounds like someone setting a table.
Six o'clock. The bell is so far away it sounds like a memory.
The bell rang six and Léo waved at the church. Busy waver.
Every table full and Marcel still remembers Léo's straw.
The terrace is humming. Léo is reading other people's menus.
A full terrace and one tiny chair for Léo. We squeeze in.
The café is packed. I will wave at Marcel and keep walking.
Listen to the terrace. Half laughter, half spoons. Lovely.
Busy lunch. Léo has made friends with the next table's baby.
The café is nearly empty. Marcel is reading. Shh, Léo.
The music started. Théo, finish your glass. You promised.
First notes under the string lights. My feet are already gone.
